## Translational Abstract

When psychologists use Bayesian statistics to test whether an experimental effect exists, for example whether a memory training improved accuracy, they must tell the software which effect sizes they consider plausible before seeing the data. This is called a prior distribution. For the most common outcome in laboratory experiments, whether a response was correct or not, the usual analysis is logistic regression, and choosing a prior for it is hard: the model works on a transformed scale, so a prior that looks harmless there can imply absurd expectations about how often participants respond correctly. This paper gives a three-step procedure for choosing such priors in a way that anyone can check, because every choice is translated back to the probability scale, where researchers can judge what is plausible for their experiment. The first step identifies a family of prior distributions that fits the mathematics of logistic regression and gives a simple reference point. The second step shows what different prior widths imply for success probabilities and for differences between conditions. The third step uses extensive simulations to show how the width of the prior changes the evidence that the Bayes factor reports, both when an effect exists and when it does not. [PENDING T5: one sentence on the main simulation result.] We state our recommended priors as transparent judgments about plausible effects, not as objective defaults, and report what they cost as well as what they gain. Ready-to-use code for the brms R package is provided.
